blocks.content: INTRODUCTION TO LIGHT

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Light exhibits a dual nature, behaving as electromagnetic waves in propagation and as discrete particles (photons) in interaction with matter.
Concave mirrors converge light and can form both real and virtual images, whereas convex mirrors diverge light and always form virtual, erect, and diminished images.
Refraction occurs due to a change in the speed of light across different optical media, following Snell's Law (n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r).
Defects of vision are corrected using specialized lenses: concave lenses for Myopia, convex lenses for Hypermetropia, and bifocal lenses for Presbyopia.
Dispersion splits white light into its component colors (VIBGYOR) because different wavelengths refract through different angles in a prism.

blocks.content: Light is a form of energy that makes objects visible to us. Without light, we cannot see anything.
Light travels in straight lines and shows many interesting phenomena such as:
Light does not require any medium to travel.
Its speed in vacuum is the highest known speed in nature. Speed of light in vacuum = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
NATURE OF LIGHT
Light behaves both as a wave and as a particle.

items:
• Wave nature explains reflection, refraction and interference.
  • Particle nature explains photoelectric effect.
Wave nature explains reflection, refraction and interference.

blocks.content: For , you only need to remember that:
Light travels in straight lines and behaves like a wave.
REFLECTION OF LIGHT
Reflection of light is the process by which light rays return back into the same medium after striking a surface.
When light falls on a smooth and polished surface, it gets reflected.
Laws of Reflection
There are two laws of reflection:

items: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.
The incident ray, reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane.

blocks.content: These laws are valid for all reflecting surfaces.
TYPES OF MIRRORS
Mirrors are smooth reflecting surfaces. There are three types of mirrors:
Plane Mirror
A plane mirror is a flat reflecting surface. Characteristics of image:

items:
• Image is virtual and erect
  • Image size is equal to object size
  • Image distance = object distance
  • Image is laterally inverted
Image size is equal to object size

blocks.content: Uses:
Concave Mirror
A concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inward. Characteristics:

items:
• It is a converging mirror
  • Can form real or virtual image
  • Real image is inverted
  • Virtual image is erect
Can form real or virtual image

blocks.content: Light travels in a straight line in a homogeneous medium, a phenomenon known as the rectilinear propagation of light.
Uses:
Convex Mirror
A convex mirror has its reflecting surface bulging outward. Characteristics:

items:
• It is a diverging mirror
  • Always forms virtual, erect and diminished image
  • Gives wide field of view
Always forms virtual, erect and diminished image

blocks.content: Uses:
REFRACTION OF LIGHT
Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one medium to another. This happens because speed of light changes in different media.
Examples:

items:
• Pencil appears bent in water
  • Coin appears raised in water

blocks.content: Laws of Refraction

items: The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane.
The ratio of sine of angle of incidence to sine of angle of refraction is constant.

Higher the refractive index, greater is the bending of light.
LENSES
A lens is a transparent object bounded by at least one curved surface. Types of lenses:
Convex Lens
A convex lens is thicker at the centre and thinner at the edges. Properties:

items:
• Converging lens
  • Can form real or virtual image
  • Used in microscope, camera, magnifying glass
Can form real or virtual image
Used in microscope, camera, magnifying glass

blocks.content: Concave Lens
A concave lens is thinner at the centre and thicker at the edges. Properties:

items:
• Diverging lens
  • Always forms virtual image
  • Used to correct myopia

blocks.content: HUMAN EYE
Human eye works like a camera. Parts of human eye:

items:
• Cornea – allows light to enter
  • Iris – controls light entering eye
  • Pupil – opening of eye
  • Lens – focuses light
  • Retina – forms image

blocks.content: Defects of Vision

items: Myopia (Short-sightedness) Cannot see distant objects clearly. Corrected by concave lens.
Hypermetropia (Long-sightedness) Cannot see nearby objects clearly. Corrected by convex lens.

blocks.content: Occurs due to ageing.
DISPERSION OF LIGHT
Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven colours. VIBGYOR:
Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red Dispersion occurs due to refraction of light.

items: Sign Convention Rules: Focal length (f) is positive for convex mirrors and lenses, but negative for concave mirrors and lenses.
Power of a Lens (P = 1 / f in meters) expressed in Dioptres (D) is a high-frequency topic in numerical problems.
Rayleigh Scattering specifies that scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength (I ∝ 1/λ⁴), explaining why the sky appears blue.

blocks.content: SCATTERING OF LIGHT
Scattering of light explains:

items:
• Blue colour of sky
  • Red colour of sun at sunrise and sunset
Red colour of sun at sunrise and sunset

blocks.content: Shorter wavelength scatters more than longer wavelength.
IMPORTANT  QUESTIONS
Q1. Speed of light in vacuum? Ans: 3 × 10⁸ m/s
Q2. Which mirror is used as rear-view mirror? Ans: Convex mirror
Q3. Which lens is used to correct myopia? Ans: Concave lens
Q4. What is refractive index?
Ans: Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to medium
